newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND MULLS CONV BONDS TO FUND PENSION REFORM.
newsitem.headline: POLAND MULLS CONV BONDS TO FUND PENSION REFORM.

text.p: The Polish government may issue convertible bonds exchangeable for shares of privatised firms to finance the crucial reform of the country's social security system, officials preparing the reform said on Wednesday.

The five to seven-year bonds, likely to be sold at a discount, could be issued in 1999 or even next year if parliament passes several crucial bills triggering the reform in 1997, treasury ministry adviser Krzysztof Pater said.
"The bonds would be available both to domestic and foreign investors," Pater, member of the team of experts preparing the pension system reform, told a news conference.

But many politicians, including Labour Minister Tadeusz Zielinski, has said party bickering before this year's parliamentary elections is likely to delay the passage of the reform plan well beyond this year.
Pater said that under his team's proposal the bonds would be exchangeable for shares in a group of about 70-80 companies with best financial results, which still remain state-owned.
Government officials have earlier said the group could include telecom monopolist TPSA, distilleries or some banks.
Pater said that under the latest proposal the bonds could be exchanged for stakes of up to 80 percent in firms undergoing privatisation.
The government has earlier said only 30-percent stakes in such companies would be used in the social security reform.

Funds raised by the bond issues would be injected to the state-owned Social Security Office (ZUS), which under the reform plan would lose part of the premiums it now gets, said Michal Rutkowski, the head of the social security reform team.

ZUS, now the sole pension provider, gets 45 percent of all officially employed workers' wages and immediately spends them on pensions. It also gets subsidies from the government which now amount to more than 15 percent of the budget's spending.

Rutkowski said that under the reform 20 percent of the premium now paid to ZUS would go to new, privately-managed pension funds, which would invest in safe securities under close government supervision.
He said people under 30 years of age at the time of the reform's implementation would pay the premium to the new funds on a mandatory basis unless a different proposal was adopted.
Apart from pensions received from ZUS and from the new funds, people could secure stipends in entirely private pension schemes, contribution to which would be tax-deductible.
Under the reform, ZUS operations will be rationalised and state subsidy to farmers' pensions and roll back privileges of some groups such as miners or the military would likely be cut.
But analysts say it remains unknown when the badly-needed but long-delayed pension system reform is implemented.

The recently appointed minister in charge of the reform, Jerzy Hausner, promised on Wednesday to meet the March deadline, set by his predecessor, for submitting to the full cabinet two pivotal bills, which would kick off the reform.
But Labour Minister Zielinski has earlier said he was not confident whether parliament would pass the bills before the elections, scheduled around September this year.

Many of Poland's nine million pensioners fear the reform would lower their incomes even though the government assures it will not, provided that Poland maintains its economic growth at more than five percent last year.
But international financial organisations have warned that Poland's public finances would face collapse in the long term if the reform is not carried out.
The aging population would increase state subsidies to the system beyond what could be borne.
